newsitem.title: JAPAN: Profits soar at Japan's Daihatsu on RV boom.
newsitem.headline: Profits soar at Japan's Daihatsu on RV boom.

text.p: A boom in recreational vehicles sent profits soaring at Japan's Daihatsu Motor Co Ltd in the first half of the fiscal year, as motorists snapped up the firm's nifty little cars.
Daihatsu, Japan's second biggest minicar maker, said on Thursday that its profits more than doubled in the six months to the end of September, rising a steep 130 percent.

Daihatsu, owned 33.4 percent by Toyota Motor Corp, unveiled a parent current profit of 5.18 billion yen ($46.2 million) for the six months to September compared with 2.29 billion ($20.4 million) a year earlier.

The company revised up its profit forecast for the full year to 13 billion yen ($116 million) from its May forecast of 11 billion yen ($98.2 million) and against an actual 9.77 billion yen ($87.2 million) profit the year before. This would be its fourth rise in annual profits in a row.
Current profit is pre-tax and includes gains and losses on securities investments and other non-operating activities.
"The great increase (in the half-year profits) was mainly due to strong demand for our Move model," a Daihatsu spokeswoman said.

The Move is a 660cc minivan-type recreational vehicle, a small but roomy model which has proved popular with drivers in congested towns and cities. Sales of sporty recreational vehicles (RVs) have been booming in Japan as customers sought a change from the traditional sedan styling.

Daihatsu's minivehicle sales, including those of mini recreational vehicles, in the half year rose nearly 19 percent to 217,000, and the company raised its sales forecast for the full year to 449,000 from its May forecast of 433,000, against actual sales of 418,000 a year earlier.

The spokeswoman said demand for the Move was still strong and the company expected its new recreational vehicle launched in August, the Pyzar, to make a good contribution to overall sales. Daihatsu launched the Pyzar with a monthly sales target of 2,500. It sold 5,800 Pyzars by the end of October.

Daihatsu also plans to introduce a two-seater version and an automatic transmission version of its existing Midget II -- a single-seater mini truck launched in April -- next spring. It will also launch a new compact recreational vehicle in the first half of 1997, Daihatsu vice president Hajime Fujii said.

Daihatsu's main market is in Japan but it also expects to benefit from the yen's fall against the dollar, which helps make its exports more price-competitive overseas. The company said it expected the weaker yen to increase its exports to 74,000 vehicles in 1996/97 against 65,000 a year earlier.

The company will raise its dividend for the second half by one yen to 2.5 yen from a year earlier, to commemorate its 90th anniversary. This would bring its total dividend to four yen for the 1996/97 year, up from three yen paid last year. It earlier planned to maintain a three yen dividend for this year. ($1=112 yen)
